sources.citation: Jacquesson, François. 2015. Persons and Grammar in Meyor (author preprint, HAL halshs-01672242, submitted 23 Dec 2017).
sources.note: Same content as the published chapter: Netan-pu 'is indeed the only one to have tones' (preprint p. 1, fn 4); dialects differ 'in prosody, lexicon, and grammar'. Nothing on stress placement.

sources.citation: Jacquesson, François. 2015. Persons and grammar in Meyor. In Mark W. Post, Stephen Morey & Scott DeLancey (eds.), Language and Culture in Northeast India and Beyond: In Honor of Robbins Burling, 100-113. Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics (A-PL 023). Handle 1885/38458.
sources.note: No phonology section and nothing on word stress. p. 101: of the three Indian-side dialects (Kaho, Walong, Netan-pu) the Netan-pu variety is 'reputed for its tunes, maybe the only one to have tones'; the dialects 'have differences in prosody, lexicon, and grammar'. fn 5: 'among Meyor where tones are the privilege of the Netan-pu'. Data are Kaho dialect. Later uses of 'stress' (pp. 101, 105, 108) mean emphasis/focus, not word accent.

sources.citation: Sun, Hongkai. 1999. On the Tibeto-Burman languages of the eastern Himalayan area in China. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 22(2): 61-72.
sources.note: First-hand report on Dza (over one thousand vocabulary items recorded in 1976): four comparative tables Dza / Geman / local Tibetan whose forms carry superscript Chao-type tone numerals (scanned-garbled in the scan, e.g. 31, 55, 53 visible), lexical percentages (20% Geman-like, 70% Tibetan-like, 7% neither) and five grammar points. It gives NO statement of the Dza tone inventory or of stress; the only phonology remark is the general 'We also worked out the phonemic systems of these languages' (p. 61, about the 1976 survey). Tone-relevant only as transcribed primary data implying lexical pitch…

tone.quote: In Dzayu county, the local people told me that there is a group named “Dza” that uses a special language, which no outsiders had any knowledge of. [...] I determined that the language of the Dza is not a new language, but rather a mixture of Geman and Tibetan in both vocabulary and grammar. [...] In the more than one thousand Dza vocabulary items recorded, slightly more than 20% are identical or similar to Geman, 70% are identical or similar to Tibetan, and about 7% are similar to neither Geman nor Tibetan.
tone.locator: pp. 64 and 66, section 3.0 'The Dza language' and 3.1 'The vocabulary'; no tone passage exists in the article

sources.note: Douban record + publisher blurb: two survey reports from Sun's 1976-82 fieldwork, arranged river basin by river basin (嘉陵江上游, 岷江, 大渡河, 雅砻江, 金沙江, 澜沧江, 怒江, 雅鲁藏布江流域; part 贰 = 川西民族走廊地区的语言), giving distribution, speaker numbers, 语言特点 and genetic position of newly found languages; the 扎话/Dza passage presumably sits in the 雅鲁藏布江流域 chapter (Zayü).
